entries.864394a2980b49ac08787d10b89fa8ea21e0ea20: <div sID="gen15955" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Isa.23" sID="Isa.23"/> <div eID="gen15955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15956" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15957" type="x-p"/> This chapter is concerning Tyre, an ancient wealthy city, situated upon the sea, and for many ages one of the most celebrated cities for trade and merchandise in those parts of the world. The lot of the tribe of Asher bordered upon it. See <reference osisRef="Josh.19.29">Joshua xix. 29</reference>, where it is called "the strong city Tyre." We seldom find it a dangerous enemy to Israel, but sometimes their faithful ally, as in the reigns of David and Solomon; for trading cities maintain their grandeur, not by the conquest of their neighbours, but by commerce with them. In this chapter is foretold, I. The lamentable desolation of Tyre, which was performed by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army, about the time that they destroyed Jerusalem; and a hard task they had of it, as appears <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">Ezek. xxix. 18</reference>, where they are said to have "served a hard service against Tyre," and yet to have no wages, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. The restoration of Tyre after seventy years, and the return of the Tyrians out of their captivity to their trade again, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15-Isa.23.18">ver. 15-18</reference>.
entries.de6ee25f9510e313d2f57344e1507c054ca84853: <div eID="gen15957" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15956" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15958" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them. <hi type="super">2</hi> Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle; thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished. <hi type="super">3</hi> And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, <hi type="italic">is</hi> her revenue; and she is a mart of nations. <hi type="super">4</hi> Be thou ashamed, O Zidon: for the sea hath spoken, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the strength of the sea, saying, I travail not, nor bring forth children, neither do I nourish up young men, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> bring up virgins. <hi type="super">5</hi> As at the report concerning Egypt, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre. <hi type="super">6</hi> Pass ye over to Tarshish; howl, ye inhabitants of the isle.   7 <hi type="italic">Is</hi> this your joyous <hi type="italic">city,</hi> whose antiquity <hi type="italic">is</hi> of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn. <hi type="super">8</hi> Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning <hi type="italic">city,</hi> whose merchants <hi type="italic">are</hi> princes, whose traffickers <hi type="italic">are</hi> the honourable of the earth? <hi type="super">9</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth. <hi type="super">10</hi> Pass through thy land as a river, O daughter of Tarshish: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no more strength. <hi type="super">11</hi> He stretched out his hand over the sea, he shook the kingdoms: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath given a commandment against the merchant <hi type="italic">city,</hi> to destroy the strong holds thereof. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon: arise, pass over to Chittim; there also shalt thou have no rest. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold the land of the Chaldeans; this people was not, <hi type="italic">till</hi> the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness: they set up the towers thereof, they raised up the palaces thereof; <hi type="italic">and</hi> he brought it to ruin. <hi type="super">14</hi> Howl, ye ships of Tarshish: for your strength is laid waste. <div eID="gen15958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15959" type="x-p"/> Tyre being a sea-port town, this prophecy of its overthrow fitly begins and ends with, <hi type="italic">Howl, you ships of Tarshish;</hi> for all its business, wealth, and honour, depended upon its shipping; if that be ruined, they will be all undone. Observe, <div eID="gen15959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15960" type="x-p"/> I. Tyre flourishing. This is taken notice of that her fall may appear the more dismal. 1. <hi type="italic">The merchants of Zidon,</hi> who traded at sea, had at first <hi type="italic">replenished her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.23.2">v. 2</reference>. Zidon was the more ancient city, situated upon the same sea-cost, a few leagues more to the north, and Tyre was at first only a colony of that; but the daughter had outgrown the mother, and become much more considerable. It may be a mortification to great cities to think how they were at first replenished. 2. Egypt had helped very much to raise her, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">v. 3</reference>. Sihor was the river of Egypt: by that river, and the ocean into which it ran, the Egyptians traded with Tyre; and the harvest of that river was her revenue. The riches of the sea, and the gains by goods exported and imported, are as much the harvest to trading towns as that of hay and corn is to the country; and sometimes <hi type="italic">the harvest of the river</hi> proves a better revenue than the harvest of the land. Or it may be meant of all the products of the Egyptian soil, which the men of Tyre traded in, and which were the harvest of the river Nile, owing themselves to the overflowing of that river. 3. She had become the mart of the nations, the great emporium of that part of the world. Some of every known nation might be found there, especially at certain times of the year, when there was a general rendezvous of merchants. This is enlarged upon by another prophet, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.2-Ezek.27.3">Ezek. xxvii. 2, 3</reference>, &c. See how the hand of the diligent, by the blessing of God upon it, makes rich. Tyre became rich and great by industry, though she had no other ploughs going than those that plough the waters. 4. She was a <hi type="italic">joyous city,</hi> noted for mirth and jollity, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">v. 7</reference>. Those that were so disposed might find there all manner of sports and diversions, all the delights of the sons and daughters of men, balls, and plays, and operas, and every thing of that kind that a man had a fancy to. This made them secure and proud, and they despised the country people, who neither knew nor relished any joys of that nature. This also made them very loth to believe and consider what warnings God gave them by his servants; they were too merry to mind them. Her <hi type="italic">antiquity</hi> likewise was <hi type="italic">of ancient days,</hi> and she was proud of that, and that helped to make her secure; as if because she had been a city time out of mind, and her antiquity had been of ancient days, therefore she must continue a city time without end, and her continuance must be to the days of eternity. 5. She was <hi type="italic">a crowning city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">v. 8</reference>), that crowned herself. Such were the power and pomp of her magistrates that they crowned those who had dependence on her and dealings with her. It is explained in the following words: <hi type="italic">Her merchants are princes,</hi> and live like princes for the ease and state they take; and <hi type="italic">her traffickers,</hi> whatever country they go to, <hi type="italic">are the honourable of the earth,</hi> who are respected by all. How slightly soever some now speak of tradesmen, it seems formerly, and among the wisest nations, there were merchants, and traders, and men of business, that were the honourable of the earth. <div eID="gen15960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15961" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Tyre falling. It does not appear that she brought trouble upon herself by provoking her neighbours with her quarrels, but rather by tempting them with her wealth; but, if it was this that induced Nebuchadnezzar to fall upon Tyre, he was disappointed; for after it had stood out a siege of thirteen years, and could hold out no longer, the inhabitants got away by sea, with their families and goods, to other places where they had an interest, and left Nebuchadnezzar nothing but the bare city. See a history of Tyre in Sir Walter Raleigh's History of the World, <hi type="italic">lib.</hi> 2. <hi type="italic">cap.</hi> 7. <hi type="italic">sect.</hi> 3, 43. <hi type="italic">page.</hi> 283, which will give much light to this prophecy and that in Ezekiel concerning Tyre. <div eID="gen15961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15962" type="x-p"/> 1. See how the destruction of Tyre is here foretold. (1.) The haven shall be no convenient harbour for the reception of the ships of Tarshish, but all <hi type="italic">laid waste</hi> (1.), so that there shall be no house, no dock for the ships to ride in, no inns, or public houses for the seamen, no entering into the port. Perhaps it was choked with sand or blocked up by the enemy. Or, Tyre being destroyed and laid waste, the ships that used to come from Tarshish and Chittim into that port shall now no more enter in; for <hi type="italic">it is revealed</hi> or made known <hi type="italic">to them,</hi> they have received the dismal news, that Tyre is destroyed and laid waste; so that there is now no more business for them there. See how it is in this world; those that are spoiled by their enemies are commonly slighted by their old friends. (2.) The inhabitants are struck with astonishment. Tyre was an island. The inhabitants of it, who had made a mighty noise and bustle in the world, and revelled with loud huzzas, shall now be still and silent (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.2">v. 2</reference>); they shall sit down as mourners, so overwhelmed with grief that they shall not be able to express it. Their proud boasts of themselves, and defiances of their neighbours, shall be silenced. God can soon quiet those, and strike them dumb, that are the noisy busy people of the world. Be still; for God will do his work (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Ps. xlvi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">Zech. ii. 13</reference>), and you cannot resist him. (3.) The neighbours are amazed, blush, and are in pain for them: <hi type="italic">Zidon is ashamed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.4">v. 4</reference>), by whom Tyre was at first replenished; for the rolling waves of the sea brought to Zidon this news from Tyre; and there <hi type="italic">the strength of the sea,</hi> a high spring-tide, proclaimed saying, "<hi type="italic">I travail not, nor bring forth children</hi> now, as I have done. I do not now, as I used to do, bring ship-loads of young people to Tyre, to be bred up there in trade and business," which was the thing that had made Tyre so rich and populous. Or the sea, that used to be loaded with fleets of ships about Tyre, shall not be as desolate as a sorrowful widow that is bereaved of all her children, and has none about her to nourish and bring up. Egypt indeed was a much larger and more considerable kingdom than Tyre was; and yet Tyre had so large a correspondence, upon the account of trade, that all the nations about shall be as much in pain, upon the report of the ruin of that one city, as they would have been, and not long after were, upon the report of the ruin of all Egypt, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.5">v. 5</reference>. Or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">When the report shall reach to the Egyptians they shall be sorely pained to hear it of Tyre,</hi> both because of the loss of their trade with that city and because it was a threatening step towards their own ruin; when their neighbour's house was on fire their own was in danger. (4.) The merchants, as many as could, should transmit their effects to other places, and abandon Tyre, where they had raised their estates, and thought they had made them sure (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You</hi> that have long been <hi type="italic">inhabitants of this isle</hi>" (for it lay off in the sea about half a mile from the continent); "It is time to howl now, for you must pass over to Tarshish. The best course you can take is to make the best of your way to Tarshish, to the sea" (to Taressus, a city in Spain; so some), "or to some other of your plantations." Those that think their mountain stands strong, and cannot be moved, will find that here they have no continuing city. <hi type="italic">The mountains shall depart and the hills be removed.</hi> (5.) Those that could not make their escape must expect no other than to be carried into captivity; for it was the way of conquerors, in those times, to take those they conquered to be bondmen in their own country, and send of their own to be freemen in theirs (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn;</hi> they shall be hurried away on foot into captivity, and many a weary step they shall take towards their own misery. Those that have lived in the greatest pomp and splendour know not what hardships they may be reduced to before they die. (6.) Many of those that attempted to escape should be pursued and fall into the hands of the enemy. Tyre shall <hi type="italic">pass through her land as a river</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.10">v. 10</reference>), running down, one company after another, into the ocean or abyss of misery. Or, though they hasten away as a river, with the greatest swiftness, hoping to outrun the danger, yet <hi type="italic">there is no more strength;</hi> they are quickly tired, and cannot get forward, but fall an easy prey into the hands of the enemy. And, as Tyre has no more strength, so her sister Zidon has no more comfort (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt no more rejoice, O oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon,</hi> that art now ready to be overpowered by the victorious Chaldeans! Thy turn is next; therefore <hi type="italic">arise; pass over to Chittim;</hi> flee to Greece, to Italy, any where to shift for thy own safety; yet <hi type="italic">there also shalt thou have no rest;</hi> thy enemies shall disturb thee, and thy own fears shall disquiet thee, where thou hopedst to find some repose." Note, We deceive ourselves if we promise ourselves rest any where in this world. Those that are uneasy in one place will be so in another; and, when God's judgments pursue sinners, they will overtake them. <div eID="gen15962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15963" type="x-p"/> 2. But whence shall all this trouble come? <div eID="gen15963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15964" type="x-p"/> (1.) God will be the author of it; it is a <hi type="italic">destruction from the Almighty.</hi> It will be asked (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">v. 8</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Who has taken this counsel against Tyre?</hi> Who has contrived it? Who has resolved it? Who can find in his heart to lay such a stately lovely city in ruins? And how is it possible that its ruin should be effected?" To this it will be answered, [1.] God has designed it, who is infinitely wise and just, and never did, nor ever will do, any wrong to any of his creatures (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">v. 9</reference>). <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts,</hi> that has all things at his disposal and gives not account of any of his matters, he <hi type="italic">has purposed it.</hi> It shall be done according to the counsel of his will; and that which he aims at herein is <hi type="italic">to stain the pride of all glory,</hi> to pollute it, profane it, and throw it to be trodden upon; <hi type="italic">and to bring into contempt</hi> and make despicable <hi type="italic">all the honourable ones of the earth,</hi> that they may not admire themselves and be admired by others as usual. God did not bring those calamities upon Tyre in a way of sovereignty, to show an arbitrary and irresistible power; but he did it to punish the Tyrians for their pride. Many other sins, no doubt, reigned among them—idolatry, sensuality, and oppression; but the sin of pride is fastened upon as that which was the particular ground of God's controversy with Tyre; for he resists the proud. All the world observing and being surprised at the desolation of Tyre, we have here an exposition of it. God tells the world what he meant by it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He designed to convince men of the vanity and uncertainty of all earthly glory, to show them what a withering, fading, perishing thing it is even when it seems most substantial. It were well if men would be thoroughly taught this lesson, though it were at the expense of so great a destruction. Are men's learning and wealth, their pomp and power, their interest in, and influence upon, all about them, their glory? Are their stately houses, rich furniture, and splendid appearances, their glory? Look up on the ruins of Tyre, and see all this glory stained, and sullied, and buried in the dust. The honourable ones of heaven will be for ever such; but see the grandees of Tyre, some fled into banishment, others forced into captivity, and all impoverished, and you will conclude that the honourable of the earth, even the most honourable, know not how soon they may be brought into contempt. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He designed hereby to prevent their being proud of that glory, their being puffed up, and confident of the continuance of it. Let the ruin of Tyre be a warning to all places and persons to take heed of pride; for it proclaims to all the world that he who exalts himself shall be abased. [2.] God will do it, who has all power in his hand and can do it effectually (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">He stretched out his hand over the sea.</hi> He has done so many a time, witness the dividing of the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh in it. He has often shaken the kingdoms that were most secure; and he has now given commandment concerning this merchant-city, to destroy the strongholds thereof. As its beauty shall not intercede for it, but that shall be stained, so its strength shall not protect it, but that shall be broken. If any think it strange that a city so well fortified, and that has so many powerful allies, should be so totally ruined, let them know that it is the Lord of hosts that has given a commandment to destroy the strongholds thereof: and who can gainsay his orders or hinder the execution of them? <div eID="gen15964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15965" type="x-p"/> (2.) The Chaldeans shall be the instruments of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold the land of the Chaldeans;</hi> how easily they and their land were destroyed by the Assyrians. Though their own hands <hi type="italic">founded it, set up the towers</hi> of Babylon, and <hi type="italic">raised up its palaces,</hi> yet the Assyrians brought it to ruin, whence the Tyrians might infer that as easily as the old Chaldeans were subdued by the Assyrians so easily shall Tyre be vanquished by those new Chaldeans. Babel was built by the Assyrians for <hi type="italic">those that dwelt in the wilderness.</hi> It may be rendered <hi type="italic">for the ships</hi> (the Assyrians founded it for ships and shipmen that traffic upon those vast rivers Tigris and Euphrates to the Persian and Indian seas), <hi type="italic">for men of the desert,</hi> for Babylon is called the <hi type="italic">desert of the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">ch. xxi. 1</reference>. Thus Tyrus was built upon the sea for the like purpose. But the Assyrians (says Dr. Lightfoot) brought that to ruin, now lately, in Hezekiah's time, and so shall Tyre hereafter be brought to ruin by Nebuchadnezzar. If we looked more upon the falling and withering of others, we should not be so confident as we commonly are of the continuance of our own flourishing and standing.
entries.549d39c5407b64ebe480f33d9d531776f5526fe9: <div eID="gen15965" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Restoration of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15966" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king: after the end of seventy years shall Tyre sing as a harlot. <hi type="super">16</hi> Take a harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it shall come to pass after the end of seventy years, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will visit Tyre, and she shall turn to her hire, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. <hi type="super">18</hi> And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing. <div eID="gen15966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15967" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The time fixed for the continuance of the desolations of Tyre, which were not to be perpetual desolations: <hi type="italic">Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15">v. 15</reference>. So long it shall lie neglected and buried in obscurity. It was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar much about the time that Jerusalem was, and lay as long as it did in its ruins. See the folly of that proud ambitious conqueror. What the richer, what the stronger, was he for making himself master of Tyre, when all the inhabitants were driven out of it and he had none of his own subjects to spare for the replenishing and fortifying of it? It is surprising to see what pleasure men could take in destroying cities and making <hi type="italic">their memorial perish with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">Ps. ix. 6</reference>. He trampled on the pride of Tyre, and therein served God's purpose; but with greater pride, for which God soon after humbled him. <div eID="gen15967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15968" type="x-p"/> II. A prophecy of the restoration of Tyre to its glory again: <hi type="italic">After the end of seventy years, according to the years of one king,</hi> or one dynasty or family of kings, that of Nebuchadnezzar; when that expired, the desolations of Tyre came to an end. And we may presume that Cyrus at the same time when he released the Jews, and encouraged them to rebuild Jerusalem, released the Tyrians also, and encouraged them to rebuild Tyre. Thus the prosperity and adversity of places, as well as persons, are <hi type="italic">set the one over against the other,</hi> that the most glorious cities may not be secure nor the most ruinous despair. It is foretold, 1. That God's providence shall gain smile upon this ruined city (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will visit Tyre</hi> in mercy; for, though he contend, he will not contend for ever. It is not said, Her old acquaintance shall visit her, the colonies she has planted, and the trading cities she has had correspondence with (they have forgotten her); but, The Lord shall visit her by some unthought-of turn; he shall cause his indignation towards her to cease, and then things will run of course in their former channel. 2. That she shall use her best endeavours to recover her trade again. She shall sing as a harlot, that has been some time under correction for her lewdness; but, when she is set at liberty (so violent is the bent of corruption), she will use her old arts of temptation. The Tyrians having returned from their captivity, and those that remained recovering new spirits thereupon, they shall contrive how to force a trade, shall procure the best choice of goods, under-sell their neighbours, and be obliging to all customers; as a harlot that has been forgotten, when she comes to be spoken of again, recommends herself to company by singing and playing, <hi type="italic">takes a harp, goes about the city,</hi> perhaps in the night, serenading, <hi type="italic">makes sweet melody, and sings many songs.</hi> These are innocent and allowable diversions, if soberly, and moderately, and modestly used; but those that value themselves upon their virtue should not be over-fond of them, nor ambitious to excel in them, because, whatever they are now, anciently they were some of the baits with which harlots used to entice fools. Tyre shall now by degrees come to be the mart of nations again; she shall <hi type="italic">return to her hire,</hi> to her traffic, <hi type="italic">and shall commit fornication</hi> (that is, she shall have dealings in trade, for the prophet carries on the similitude of a harlot) <hi type="italic">with all the kingdoms of the world</hi> that she had formerly traded with in her prosperity. The love of worldly wealth is a spiritual whoredom, and therefore covetous people are called <hi type="italic">adulterers and adulteresses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">James iv. 4</reference>), and covetousness is spiritual idolatry. 3. That, having recovered her trade again, she shall make a better use of it than she had done formerly; and this good she should get by her calamities (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her merchandise, and her hire, shall be holiness to the Lord.</hi> The trade of Tyre, and all the gains of her trade, shall be devoted to God and to his honour and employed in his service. It shall not be treasured and hoarded up, as formerly, to be the matter of their pride and the support of their carnal confidence; but it shall be laid out in acts of piety and charity. What they can spare from the maintenance of themselves and their families <hi type="italic">shall be for those that dwell before the Lord,</hi> for the priests, the Lord's ministers, that attend in his temple at Jerusalem; not to maintain them in pomp and grandeur, but that they and theirs may <hi type="italic">eat sufficiently,</hi> may have food convenient for them, with as little as may be of that care which would divert them from their ministration, and that they may have, not rich and fine clothing, but <hi type="italic">durable clothing,</hi> that which is strong and lasting, <hi type="italic">clothing for old men</hi> (so some read it), as if the priests, though they were young, must wear such plain grave clothing as old men used to wear. Now, (1.) This supposes that religion should be set up in New Tyre, that they should come to the knowledge of the true God and into communion with the Israel of God. Perhaps their being fellow-captives with the Jews in Babylon (who had prophets with them there) disposed them to join with them in their worship there, and turned them from idols, as it cured the Jews of their idolatry: and when they were released with them, and as they had reason to believe for their sakes, when they were settled again in Tyre, they would send gifts and offerings to the temple, and presents to the priests. We find men of Tyre then dwelling in the land of Judah, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.16">Neh. xiii. 16</reference>. Tyre and Sidon were better disposed to religion in Christ's time than the cities of Israel; for, if Christ had gone among them, <hi type="italic">they would have repented,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">Matt. xi. 21</reference>. And we meet with Christians at Tyre (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.3-Acts.21.4">Acts xxi. 3, 4</reference>), and, many years after, did Christianity flourish there. Some of the rabbin refer this prophecy of the conversion of Tyre to the days of the Messiah. (2.) It directs those that have estates to make use of them in the service of God and religion, and to reckon that best laid up which is so laid out. Both the merchandise of the tradesmen and the hire of the day-labourers shall be devoted to God. Both the merchandise (the employment we follow) and the hire (the gain of our employments) must <hi type="italic">be holiness to the Lord,</hi> alluding to the motto engraven on the frontlet of the high priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.30">Exod. xxxix. 30</reference>), and to the separation of the tithe under the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30">Lev. xxvii. 30</reference>. See a promise like this referring to gospel times, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.20-Zech.14.21">Zech. xiv. 20, 21</reference>. We must first give up ourselves to be holiness to the Lord before what we do, or have, or get, can be so. When we abide with God in our particular callings, and do common actions after a godly sort—when we abound in works of piety and charity, are liberal in relieving the poor, and supporting the ministry, and encouraging the gospel—then our merchandise and our hire are holiness to the Lord, if we sincerely look at his glory in them. And our wealth need not be treasured and laid up on earth; for it is treasured and laid up in heaven, in <hi type="italic">bags that wax not old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Luke xii. 33</reference>.  <chapter eID="Isa.23"/> <div eID="gen15968" type="x-p"/>

entries.484a19dab76dc6cffd6d644e0f5ab36eadac2a6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8717"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>. Prophecy Respecting Tyre.</title> <div sID="gen14427" type="x-p"/> Menander, the historian, notices a siege of Tyre by Shalmaneser, about the time of the siege of Samaria. Sidon, Acco, and Old Tyre, on the mainland, were soon reduced; but New Tyre, on an island half a mile from the shore, held out for five years. Sargon probably finished the siege. Sennacherib does not, however, mention it among the cities which the Assyrian kings conquered (thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh chapters). The expression, "Chaldeans" (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Is 23:13</reference>), may imply reference to its siege under Nebuchadnezzar, which lasted thirteen years. Alexander the Great destroyed New Tyre after a seven months' siege.<div eID="gen14427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8717"/><hi type="bold">1. Tyre--</hi>Hebrew, Tsur, that is, "Rock."<div eID="gen14428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ships of Tarshish--</hi>ships of Tyre returning from their voyage to Tarshish, or Tartessus in Spain, with which the Phoenicians had much commerce (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12-Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:12-25</reference>). "Ships of Tarshish" is a phrase also used of large and distant-voyaging merchant vessels (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.16">Is 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.22">1Ki 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no house--</hi>namely, left; such was the case as to Old Tyre, after Nebuchadnezzar's siege.<div eID="gen14430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no entering--</hi>There is no house to enter (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.10">Is 24:10</reference>) [G. V. Smith]. Or, Tyre is so laid waste, that there is no possibility of entering the harbor [Barnes]; which is appropriate to the previous "ships."<div eID="gen14431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim--</hi>Cyprus, of which the cities, including Citium in the south (whence came "Chittim"), were mostly Phoenician (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.6">Eze 27:6</reference>). The ships from Tarshish on their way to Tyre learn the tidings ("it is revealed to them") of the downfall of Tyre. At a later period Chittim denoted the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Da 11:30</reference>). <div eID="gen14432" type="x-p"/>
entries.af6bf423377686bc4d30fa43516c0c6e045be39c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8718"/><div sID="gen14433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8718"/><hi type="bold">2. Be still--</hi>"struck dumb with awe." Addressed to those already in the country, eye-witnesses of its ruin (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">La 2:10</reference>); or, in contrast to the busy din of commerce once heard in Tyre; now all is hushed and still.<div eID="gen14433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">isle--</hi>strictly applicable to New Tyre: in the sense coast, to the mainland city, Old Tyre (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.6">Is 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.6">Is 20:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zidon--</hi>of which Tyre was a colony, planted when Zidon was conquered by the Philistines of Ascalon. Zidon means a "fishing station"; this was its beginning.<div eID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">replenished--</hi>with wealth and an industrious population (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">Eze 27:3</reference>, 8, 23). Here "Zidon," as the oldest city of Phoenicia, includes all the Phoenician towns on the strip of "coast." Thus, Eth-baal, king of Tyre [Josephus, Antiquities, 8.3,2], is called king of the Sidonians (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">1Ki 16:31</reference>); and on coins Tyre is called the metropolis of the Sidonians. <div eID="gen14436" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dc1fd09e7edc00b05b56d1783fe52a94056fcd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8719"/><div sID="gen14437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8719"/><hi type="bold">3. great waters--</hi>the wide waters of the sea.<div eID="gen14437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seed--</hi>"grain," or crop, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.15">1Sa 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.12">Job 39:12</reference>.<div eID="gen14438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sihor--</hi>literally, "dark-colored"; applied to the Nile, as the Egyptian Jeor, and the Greek Melas, to express the "dark, turbid" colors given to its waters by the fertilizing soil which it deposits at its yearly overflow (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jr 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">harvest of the river--</hi>the growth of the Delta; the produce due to the overflow of the Nile: Egypt was the great granary of corn in the ancient world (Ge 41:1-57; 42:1-38; 43:1-34).<div eID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her revenue--</hi>Tyrian vessels carried Egyptian produce obtained in exchange for wine, oil, glass, &c., into various lands, and so made large profits.<div eID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">Eze 27:3</reference>). No city was more favorably situated for commerce. <div eID="gen14442" type="x-p"/>
entries.748ea949e2b771b3b9c6473be346c14519e89089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8720"/><div sID="gen14443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8720"/><hi type="bold">4. Zidon--</hi>called on, as being the parent country of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Is 23:12</reference>), and here equivalent to Phoenicia in general, to feel the shame (as it was esteemed in the East) of being now as childless as if she never had any. "I (no more now) travail, nor bring forth," &c. "Strength of the sea," that is, stronghold, namely, New Tyre, on a rock (as "Tyre" means) surrounded by the sea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">Eze 26:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14-Ezek.26.17">14-17</reference>; so Venice was called "Bride of the sea"; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.3">Zec 9:3</reference>). <div eID="gen14443" type="x-p"/>
entries.d283c4f0766925f8b8d59043ff15887e4a5e8766: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8721"/><div sID="gen14444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8721"/><hi type="bold">5. As, &c.--</hi>rather, "When the report (shall reach) the people of Egypt, they shall be sorely pained at the report concerning Tyre" (namely, its overthrow). So Jerome, "When the Egyptians shall hear that so powerful a neighboring nation has been destroyed, they must know their own end is near" [Lowth, &c.]. <div eID="gen14444" type="x-p"/>
entries.1198efc3c1e0d3aa19beb0591733237313f2a40b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8722"/><div sID="gen14445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8722"/><hi type="bold">6. Pass ... over--</hi>Escape from Tyre to your colonies as Tarshish (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Is 23:12</reference>). The Tyrians fled to Carthage and elsewhere, both at the siege under Nebuchadnezzar and that under Alexander. <div eID="gen14445" type="x-p"/>
entries.007e0aaf383d250a048e0c4a8a9e34bb546765bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8723"/><div sID="gen14446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8723"/>7. Is this silent ruin all that is left of your once joyous city (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Is 23:12</reference>)?<div eID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">antiquity--</hi>The Tyrian priests boasted in Herodotus' time that their city had already existed 2300 years: an exaggeration, but still implying that it was ancient even then.<div eID="gen14447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her own feet--</hi>walking on foot as captives to an enemy's land. <div eID="gen14448" type="x-p"/>
entries.1617580804a964abe786b7d6b0c882810d63cd05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8724"/><div sID="gen14449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8724"/><hi type="bold">8. Who--</hi>answered in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">Is 23:9</reference>, "The Lord of hosts."<div eID="gen14449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crowning--</hi>crown-giving; that is, the city from which dependent kingdoms had arisen, as Tartessus in Spain, Citium in Cyprus, and Carthage in Africa (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.33">Eze 27:33</reference>).<div eID="gen14450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">traffickers--</hi>literally, "Canaanites," who were famed for commerce (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">Ho 12:7</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen14451" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca46bd404ee61754b11b5eb58049edc92cff7520: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8725"/><div sID="gen14452" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8725"/>9. Whoever be the instruments in overthrowing haughty sinners, God, who has all hosts at His command, is the First Cause (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.7">Is 10:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen14452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stain--</hi>rather, "to profane"; as in <reference osisRef="Exod.31.14">Ex 31:14</reference>, the Sabbath, and other objects of religious reverence; so here, "the pride of all glory" may refer to the Tyrian temple of Hercules, the oldest in the world, according to Arrian (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.16">Is 2:16</reference>); the prophet of the true God would naturally single out for notice the idol of Tyre [G. V. Smith]. It may, however, be a general proposition; the destruction of Tyre will exhibit to all how God mars the luster of whatever is haughty (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Is 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen14453" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd4ba647fcb4a31b4e7f99d75eb3f0734ac5bb13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8726"/><div sID="gen14454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8726"/><hi type="bold">10. a river--</hi>Hebrew, "the river," namely, Nile.<div eID="gen14454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter of Tarshish--</hi>Tyre and its inhabitants (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>), about henceforth, owing to the ruin of Tyre, to become inhabitants of its colony, Tartessus: they would pour forth from Tyre, as waters flow on when the barriers are removed [Lowth]. Rather, Tarshish, or Tartessus and its inhabitants, as the phrase usually means: they had been kept in hard bondage, working in silver and lead mines near Tarshish, by the parent city (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">Eze 26:17</reference>): but now "the bond of restraint" (for so "strength," Margin, "girdle," that is, bond, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">Psa 2:3</reference>, ought to be translated) is removed, since Tyre is no more. <div eID="gen14455" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b589bcfa0f034fd07b04bd2fe1845a95ce726bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8727"/><div sID="gen14456" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8727"/><hi type="bold">11. He--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen14456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kingdoms--</hi>the Phoenician cities and colonies.<div eID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the merchant city--</hi>rather, Canaan, meaning the north of it, namely, Phoenicia. On their coins, they call their country Canaan. <div eID="gen14458" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fc13fa19af65d6d1230bb59ba55a9d0324cb083: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8728"/><div sID="gen14459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8728"/><hi type="bold">12. he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice--</hi>riotously (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">Is 23:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppressed--</hi>"deflowered"; laying aside the figure "taken by storm"; the Arabs compare a city never taken to an undefiled virgin (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen14461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter of Zidon--</hi>Tyre: or else, sons of Zidon, that is, the whole land and people of Phoenicia (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.2">Is 23:2</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen14462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim--</hi>Citium in Cyprus (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Is 23:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there also ... no rest--</hi>Thy colonies, having been harshly treated by thee, will now repay thee in kind (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.10">Is 23:10</reference>). But Vitringa refers it to the calamities which befell the Tyrians in their settlements subsequently, namely, Sicily, Corcyra, Carthage, and Spain, all flowing from the original curse of Noah against the posterity of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25-Gen.9.27">Ge 9:25-27</reference>). <div eID="gen14464" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa63d07cb74bda3941e7cc8a6faf811b280b2a69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8729"/><div sID="gen14465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8729"/><hi type="bold">13. Behold--</hi>Calling attention to the fact, so humiliating to Tyre, that a people of yesterday, like the Chaldees, should destroy the most ancient of cities, Tyre.<div eID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was not--</hi>had no existence as a recognized nation; the Chaldees were previously but a rude, predatory people (<reference osisRef="Job.1.17">Job 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen14466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Assyrian founded it--</hi>The Chaldees ("them that dwell in the wilderness") lived a nomadic life in the mountains of Armenia originally (Arphaxad, in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Ge 10:22</reference>, refers to such a region of Assyria near Armenia), north and east of Assyria proper. Some may have settled in Mesopotamia and Babylonia very early and given origin to the astrologers called Chaldees in later times. But most of the people had been transferred only a little before the time of this prophecy from their original seats in the north to Mesopotamia, and soon afterwards to South Babylonia. "Founded it," means "assigned it (the land) to them who had (heretofore) dwelt in the wilderness" as a permanent settlement (so in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.8">Psa 104:8</reference>) [Maurer]. It was the Assyrian policy to infuse into their own population of the plain the fresh blood of hardy mountaineers, for the sake of recruiting their armies. Ultimately the Chaldees, by their powerful priest-caste, gained the supremacy and established the later or Chaldean empire. Horsley refers it to Tyre, founded by an Assyrian race.<div eID="gen14467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">towers thereof--</hi>namely, of Babylon, whose towers, Herodotus says, were "set up" by the Assyrians [Barnes]. Rather, "The Chaldees set up their siege-towers" against Tyre, made for the attack of high walls, from which the besiegers hurled missiles, as depicted in the Assyrian sculptures [G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen14468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raised up--</hi>rather, "They lay bare," namely, the foundations of "her (Tyre's) palaces," that is, utterly overthrew them (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>). <div eID="gen14469" type="x-p"/>
entries.374812f286c9d1d16b5a9b919071bd5e3a57dd0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8730"/><div sID="gen14470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8730"/><hi type="bold">14. strength--</hi>stronghold (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15-Ezek.26.18">Eze 26:15-18</reference>). <div eID="gen14470" type="x-p"/>
entries.d17f6fe0f696245dfc925b0bf0499af0f36dbe92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8731"/><div sID="gen14471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8731"/><hi type="bold">15. forgotten--</hi>Having lost its former renown, Tyre shall be in obscurity.<div eID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seventy years--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">days of one king--</hi>that is, a dynasty. The Babylonian monarchy lasted properly but seventy years. From the first year of Nebuchadnezzar to the taking of Babylon, by Cyrus, was seventy years; then the subjected nations would be restored to liberty. Tyre was taken in the middle of that period, but it is classed in common with the rest, some conquered sooner and others later, all, however, alike to be delivered at the end of the period. So "king" is used for dynasty (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Da 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">8:20</reference>): Nebuchadnezzar, his son Evil-merodach, and his grandson, Belshazzar, formed the whole dynasty (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">27:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall Tyre sing as ... harlot--</hi>It shall be to Tyre as the song of the harlot, namely, a harlot that has been forgotten, but who attracts notice again by her song. Large marts of commerce are often compared to harlots seeking many lovers, that is, they court merchants of all nations, and admit any one for the sake of gain (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.4">Na 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.3">Re 18:3</reference>). Covetousness is closely akin to idolatry and licentiousness, as the connection (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>) proves (compare Is 2:6-8, 16). <div eID="gen14474" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7479eae2121f51fb4f742b850e7562ba019c6a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8732"/><div sID="gen14475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8732"/>16. Same figure [Is 23:15] to express that Tyre would again prosper and attract commercial intercourse of nations to her, and be the same joyous, self-indulging city as before. <div eID="gen14475" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e5103f06b12ca4a6d0fae89d1332f4a492d03f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8733"/><div sID="gen14476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8733"/><hi type="bold">17. visit--</hi>not in wrath, but mercy.<div eID="gen14476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hire--</hi>image from a harlot: her gains by commerce. After the Babylonian dynasty was ended, Tyre was rebuilt; also, again, after the destruction under Alexander. <div eID="gen14477" type="x-p"/>
entries.6feca744d9da160928e70d64bbe0f9b7ba9648bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8734"/><div sID="gen14478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8734"/><hi type="bold">18. merchandise ... holiness--</hi>Her traffic and gains shall at last (long after the restoration mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Is 23:17</reference>) be consecrated to Jehovah. Jesus Christ visited the neighborhood of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.21">Mt 15:21</reference>); Paul found disciples there (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.3-Acts.21.6">Ac 21:3-6</reference>); it early became a Christian bishopric, but the full evangelization of that whole race, as of the Ethiopians (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Is 18:1-7</reference>), of the Egyptians and Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">Is 19:1-25</reference>), is yet to come (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not treasured--</hi>but freely expended in His service.<div eID="gen14479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that dwell before the Lord--</hi>the ministers of religion. But Horsley translates, "them that sit before Jehovah" as disciples.<div eID="gen14480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">durable clothing--</hi>Changes of raiment constituted much of the wealth of former days. <chapter eID="Isa.23"/>

entries.71e4c284357210354a6567ea5f7df708b36e9986: <div eID="gen27418" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27419" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27420" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27420" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27419" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27421" type="x-p"/> Prophecy denouncing the destruction of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar, delivered upwards of one hundred and twenty years before its accomplishment, at a period when the Tyrians were in great prosperity, and the Babylonians in abject subjection to the Assyrian empire; and, consequently, when an event of so great magnitude was improbable in the highest degree, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.14">Isa 23:1-14</reference>. Tyre shall recover its splendor at the termination of seventy years, the days of One king, or kingdom, by which must be meant the time allotted for the duration of the Babylonish empire, as otherwise the prophecy cannot be accommodated to the event, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15-Isa.23.17">Isa 23:15-17</reference>. Supposed reference to the early conversion of Tyre to Christianity, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa 23:18</reference>. <div eID="gen27421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> The burden of Tyre - Tyre, a city on the coast of Syria, about lat. 32 N. was built two thousand seven hundred and sixty years before Christ. There were two cities of this name; one on the continent, and the other on an island, about half a mile from the shore; the city on the island was about four miles in circumference. Old Tyre resisted Nebuchadnezzar for thirteen years; then the inhabitants carried, so to speak, the city to the forementioned island, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.4">Isa 23:4</reference>. This new city held out against Alexander the Great for seven months; who, in order to take it, was obliged to fill up the channel which separated it from the main land. In a.d. 1289 it was totally destroyed by the sultan of Egypt; and now contains only a few huts, in which about fifty or sixty wretched families exist. This desolation was foretold by this prophet and by Ezekiel, one thousand nine hundred years before it took place! <div eID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27424" type="x-p"/> Howl, ye ships of Tarshish - This prophecy denounces the destruction of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar. It opens with an address to the Tyrian negotiators and sailors at Tarshish, (Tartessus, in Spain), a place which, in the course of their trade, they greatly frequented. The news of the destruction of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar is said to be brought to them from Chittim, the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean; "for the Tyrians," says Jerome on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.6">Isa 23:6</reference>, "when they saw they had no other means of escaping, fled in their ships, and took refuge in Carthage and in the islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea." From whence the news would spread and reach Tarshish; so also Jarchi on the same place. This seems to be the most probable interpretation of this verse.
entries.0552fcffa344e21a018a16032274969f7f553202: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> Be still "Be silent" - Silence is a mark of grief and consternation. See <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">Isa 47:5</reference>. Jeremiah has finely expressed this image: - "The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground, they are silent: <div eID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27426" type="x-p"/> They have cast up dust on their heads, they have girded themselves with sackcloth. <div eID="gen27426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27427" type="x-p"/> The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground." <reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">Lam 2:10</reference>.
entries.63ee74509f41940323df6d1797495846cc5570b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27428" type="x-p"/> The seed of Sihor "The seed of the Nile" - The Nile is called here Shichor, as it is <reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jer 2:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1Chr 13:5</reference>. It had this name from the blackness of its waters, charged with the mud which it brings down from Ethiopia when it overflows, Et viridem Aegyptum nigra fecundat arena; as it was called by the Greeks Melas, and by the Latins Melo, for the same reason. See Servius on the above line of Virgil, Georg. 4:291. It was called Siris by the Ethiopians, by some supposed to be the same with Shichor. Egypt by its extraordinary fertility, caused by the overflowing of the Nile supplied the neighboring nations with corn, by which branch of trade the Tyrians gained great wealth.
entries.72db8640f579b1b37b9de8c5b4f37242bf7d58b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27429" type="x-p"/> Be thou ashamed, O Zidon - Tyre is called <reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Isa 23:12</reference>, the daughter of Sidon. "The Sidonians," says Justin, 18:3, "when their city was taken by the king of Ascalon, betook themselves to their ships, and landed, and built by Tyre." Sidon, as the mother city is supposed to be deeply affected with the calamity of her daughter. <div eID="gen27429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27430" type="x-p"/> Nor bring up virgins "Nor educated virgins" - ורוממתי veromamti; so an ancient MS. Of Dr. Kennicott's prefixing the ו vau, which refers to the negative preceding, and is equivalent to ולא velo. See <reference osisRef="Deu.23.6">Deu 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.30.3">Pro 30:3</reference>. Two of my own MSS. have ו vau in the margin.
entries.0ee662ad5cb4033f4ada22b8b5ca4dae9adf5038: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27431" type="x-p"/> Whose antiquity is of ancient days "Whose antiquity is of the earliest date" - Justin, in the passage above quoted, had dated the building of Tyre at a certain number of years before the taking of Troy; but the number is lost in the present copies. Tyre, though not so old as Sidon, was yet of very high antiquity: it was a strong city even in the time of Joshua. It is called עיר מבצר צר ir mibtsar tsor, "the city of the fortress of Sor," <reference osisRef="Jos.19.29">Jos 19:29</reference>. Interpreters raise difficulties in regard to this passage, and will not allow it to have been so ancient; with what good reason I do not see, for it is called by the same name, "the fortress of Sor," in the history of David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.7">2Sam 24:7</reference>, and the circumstances of the history determine the place to be the very same. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen27431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27432" type="x-p"/> Whose antiquity is of ancient days, may refer to Palaetyrus, or Old Tyre. <div eID="gen27432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27433" type="x-p"/> Her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn - This may belong to the new or insular Tyre; her own feet, that is, her own inhabitants, shall carry her - shall transport the city, from the continent to the island. "But the text says it shall be carried far off, and the new city was founded only half a mile distant from the other." I answer, מרחוק merachok does not always signify a great distance, but distance or interval in general; for in <reference osisRef="Jos.3.4">Jos 3:4</reference> רחוק rachok is used to express the space between the camp and the ark, which we know to have been only two thousand cubits. Some refer the sojourning afar off to the extent of the commercial voyages undertaken by the Tyrians and their foreign connections.
entries.3ccfa03f62d372aaf669fd9e66d4c691478d13a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27434" type="x-p"/> O daughter of Tarshish - Tyre is called the daughter of Tarshish; perhaps because, Tyre being ruined, Tarshish was become the superior city, and might be considered as the metropolis of the Tyrian people; or rather because of the close connection and perpetual intercourse between them, according to that latitude of signification in which the Hebrews use the words son and daughter to express any sort of conjunction and dependence whatever. מזח mezach, a girdle, which collects, binds, and keeps together the loose raiment, when applied to a river, may mean a mound, mole, or artificial dam, which contains the waters and prevents them from spreading abroad. A city taken by siege and destroyed, whose walls are demolished, whose policy is dissolved, whose wealth is dissipated, whose people is scattered over the wide country, is compared to a river whose banks are broken down, and whose waters, let loose and overflowing all the neighboring plains, are wasted and lost. This may possibly be the meaning of this very obscure verse, of which I can find no other interpretation that is at all satisfactory. - L.
entries.a6730943370fd68719ba211d4b8af2b02a4a8b5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27435" type="x-p"/> Behold the land of the Chaldeans - This verse is extremely obscure; the obscurity arises from the ambiguity of the agents, which belong to the verbs, and of the objects expressed by the pronouns; from the change of number of the verbs, and of gender in the pronouns. The MSS. give us no assistance, and the ancient Versions very little. The Chaldee and Vulgate read שמוה samoah, in the plural number. I have followed the interpretation which, among many different ones, seemed to be most probable, that of Perizonius and Vitringa. <div eID="gen27435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27436" type="x-p"/> The Chaldeans, Chasdim, are supposed to have had their origin, and to have taken their name, from Chesed, the son of Nachor, the brother of Abraham. They were known by that name in the time of Moses, who calls Ur in Mesopotamia, from whence Abraham came, to distinguish it from other places of the same name, Ur of the Chaldeans. And Jeremiah calls them an ancient nation. This is not inconsistent with what Isaiah here says of them: "This people was not," that is, they were of no account, (see <reference osisRef="Deu.32.21">Deu 32:21</reference>); they were not reckoned among the great and potent nations of the world till of later times; they were a rude, uncivilized, barbarous people, without laws, without settled habitations; wandering in a wide desert country (ציים tsiyim) and addicted to rapine like the wild Arabians. Such they are represented to have been in the time of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.1.17">Job 1:17</reference>, and such they continued to be till Assur, some powerful king of Assyria, gathered them together, and settled them in Babylon in the neighboring country. This probably was Ninus, whom I suppose to have lived in the time of the Judges. In this, with many eminent chronologers, I follow the authority of Herodotus, who says that the Assyrian monarchy lasted but five hundred and twenty years. Ninus got possession of Babylon from the Cuthean Arabians; the successors of Nimrod in that empire collected the Chaldeans, and settled a colony of them there to secure the possession of the city, which he and his successors greatly enlarged and ornamented. They had perhaps been useful to him in his wars, and might be likely to be farther useful in keeping under the old inhabitants of that city, and of the country belonging to it; according to the policy of the Assyrian kings, who generally brought new people into the conquered countries; see <reference osisRef="Isa.36.17">Isa 36:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Kgs 17:24</reference>. The testimony of Dicaearchus, a Greek historian contemporary with Alexander, (apud. Steph. de Urbibus, in voc. Χαλδαιος), in regard to the fact is remarkable, though he is mistaken in the name of the king he speaks of. He says that "a certain king of Assyria, the fourteenth in succession from Ninus, (as he might be, if Ninus is placed, as in the common chronology, eight hundred years higher than we have above set him), named, as it is said, Chaldaeus, having gathered together and united all the people called Chaldeans, built the famous city, Babylon, upon the Euphrates." - L.
entries.06ddac8a34797d12fef59cadd3638e07ec544a01: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27437" type="x-p"/> Howl, ye shops - The Prophet Ezekiel hath enlarged upon this part of the same subject with great force and elegance: - "Thus saith the Lord Jehovah concerning Tyre: - <div eID="gen27437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27438" type="x-p"/> At the sound of thy fall, at the cry of the wounded, <div eID="gen27438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27439" type="x-p"/> At the great slaughter in the midst of thee, shall not the islands tremble? <div eID="gen27439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27440" type="x-p"/> And shall not all the princes of the sea descend from their thrones, <div eID="gen27440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27441" type="x-p"/> And lay aside their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments? <div eID="gen27441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27442" type="x-p"/> They shall clothe themselves with trembling, they shall sit on the ground; <div eID="gen27442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27443" type="x-p"/> They shall tremble every moment, they shall be astonished at thee. <div eID="gen27443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27444" type="x-p"/> And they shall utter a lamentation over thee, and shall say unto thee: <div eID="gen27444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27445" type="x-p"/> How art thou lost, thou that wast inhabited from the seas! <div eID="gen27445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27446" type="x-p"/> The renowned city, that was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants! <div eID="gen27446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> That struck with terror all her neighbors! <div eID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27448" type="x-p"/> Now shall the coasts tremble in the day of thy fall, <div eID="gen27448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27449" type="x-p"/> And the isles that are in the sea shall be troubled at thy departure." <reference osisRef="Eze.26.15-Eze.26.18">Eze 26:15-18</reference>.
entries.09282dc1165cf956af042e33e7b4beaffc9fca58: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27450" type="x-p"/> According to the days of one king - What is, of one kingdom; see <reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Dan 7:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">Dan 8:20</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar began his conquests in the first year of his reign; from thence to the taking of Babylon by Cyrus are seventy years, at which time the nations subdued by Nebuchadnezzar were to be restored to liberty. These seventy years limit the duration of the Babylonish monarchy. Tyre was taken by him towards the middle of that period; so did not serve the king of Babylon during the whole period, but only for the remaining part of it. This seems to be the meaning of Isaiah; the days allotted to the one king or kingdom, are seventy years; Tyre, with the rest of the conquered nations, shall continue in a state of subjection and desolation to the end of that period. Not from the beginning and through the whole of the period; for, by being one of the latest conquests, the duration of that state of subjection in regard to her, was not much more than half of it. "All these nations," saith Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jer 25:11</reference>, "shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years." Some of them were conquered sooner, some later; but the end of this period was the common term for the deliverance of them all. <div eID="gen27450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27451" type="x-p"/> There is another way of computing the seventy years, from the year in which Tyre was actually taken to the nineteenth of Darius Hystaspis; whom the Phoenicians, or Tyrians, assisted against the Ionians, and probably on that account might then be restored to their former liberties and privileges. But I think the former the more probable interpretation. - L. <div eID="gen27451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27452" type="x-p"/> Sing as a harlot - Fidicinam esse meretricum est. says Donatus in Terent. Eunuch. 3:2, 4. <div eID="gen27452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27453" type="x-p"/> Nec meretrix tibicina, cujus Ad strepitum salias. <div eID="gen27453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27454" type="x-p"/> Hor. 1:Epist. 14:25. "Nor harlot minstrel sings, when the rude sound <div eID="gen27454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27455" type="x-p"/> Tempts you with heavy heels to thump the ground." <div eID="gen27455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27456" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen27456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27457" type="x-p"/> Sir John Chardin, in his MS. note on this place, says: - <div eID="gen27457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27458" type="x-p"/> C'est que les vielles prostituees, - ne font que chanter quand les jeunes dancent, et les animer par l'instrument et par la voix. "The old prostitutes do nothing but sing, while the young ones dance; and animate them both by vocal and instrumental music."
entries.67d50b8ee36b7b9991c6c3f4f7537ad634af5d35: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27459" type="x-p"/> After the end of seventy years - Tyre, after its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, recovered, as it is here foretold, its ancient trade, wealth, and grandeur; as it did likewise after a second destruction by Alexander. It became Christian early with the rest of the neighboring countries. St. Paul himself found many Christians there, <reference osisRef="Act.21.4">Act 21:4</reference>. It suffered much in the Diocletian persecution. It was an archbishopric under the patriarchate of Jerusalem, with fourteen bishoprics under its jurisdiction. It continued Christian till it was taken by the Saracens in 639; was recovered by the Christians in 1124; but in 1280 was conquered by the Mamelukes, and afterwards taken from them by the Turks in 1517. Since that time it has sunk into utter decay; is now a mere ruin, a bare rock, "a place to spread nets upon," as the Prophet Ezekiel foretold it should be, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.14">Eze 26:14</reference>. See Sandy's Travels; Vitringa on the place; Bp. Newton on the Prophecies, Dissert. xi.  <chapter eID="Isa.23"/> <div eID="gen27459" type="x-p"/>

entries.51826c0976ac4fdb2edf88455f94012c6255badc: <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference> <div eID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13107" type="x-p"/> The prophecy commences by introducing the trading vessels of Phoenicia on their return home, as they hear with alarm the tidings of the fate that has befallen their home. <hi type="italic">“Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entrance any more! Out of the land of the Chittaeans it is made known to them.”</hi> Even upon the open sea they hear of it as a rumour from the ships that they meet. For their voyage is a very long one: they come from the Phoenician colony on the Spanish Baetis, or the Guadalquivir, as it was called from the time of the occupation by the Moors. “<hi type="italic">Ships of Tarshish</hi>” are ships that sail to Tartessus (lxx inaccurately, πλοῖα Καρχηδόνος). It is not improbable that the whole of the Mediterranean may have been called “the sea to Tarshish;” and hence the rendering adopted by the Targum, Jerome, Luther, and others, <hi type="italic">naves maris</hi> (see Humboldt, <hi type="italic">Kosmos</hi>, ii. 167, 415). These ships are to howl (<hi type="italic">hēlı̄lū</hi> instead of the feminine, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">Isa 32:11</reference>) because of the devastation that has taken place (it is easy to surmise that Tyre has been the victim); for the home and harbour, which the sailors were rejoicing at the prospect of being able to enter once more, have both been swept away. Cyprus was the last station on this homeward passage. The <hi type="italic">Chittim</hi> (written in the legends of coins and other inscriptions with <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> and <hi type="italic">Cheth</hi>) are the inhabitants of the Cyprian harbour of <hi type="italic">Citium</hi> and its territory. But Epiphanius, the bishop of Salamis in the island of Cyprus, says that Citium was also used as a name for the whole island, or even in a still broader sense. Cyprus, the principal mart of the Phoenicians, was the last landing-place. As soon as they touch the island, the fact which they have only heard of as a rumour upon the open sea, is fully disclosed (<hi type="italic">niglâh</hi>), i.e., it now becomes a clear undoubted certainty, for they are told of it by eye-witnesses who have made their escape to the island. The prophet now turns to the Phoenicians at home, who have this devastation in prospect.
entries.18c3c606f3b26dbbba8b19c307d397b59517a5a4: <reference osisRef="Isa.23.2-Isa.23.3">Isa 23:2-3</reference> <hi type="italic">“Be alarmed, ye inhabitants of the coast! Sidonian merchants, sailing over the sea, filled thee once. And the sowing of Sichor came upon great waters, the harvest of the Nile, her store; and she became gain for nations.”</hi> The suffixes of מלּא (to fill with wares and riches) and תּבוּאה (the bringing in, viz., into barns and granaries) refer to the word א<hi type="italic">י</hi>, which is used here as a feminine for the name of a country, and denotes the Phoenician coast, including the insular Tyre. “<hi type="italic">Sidonian merchants</hi>” are the Phoenicians generally, as in Homer; for the “great Sidon” of antiquity (<hi type="italic">Zidon</hi> <hi type="italic">rabbâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.8">Jos 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.28">Jos 19:28</reference>) was the mother-city of Phoenicia, which so thoroughly stamped its name upon the whole nation, that Tyre is called צדנם אם upon Phoenician coins. The meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Isa 23:3</reference></hi> is not that the revenue of Tyre which accrued to it on the great unfruitful sea, was like a Nile-sowing, or an Egyptian harvest (Hitzig, Knobel). Such a simile would be a very beautiful one, but it is a very unlikely one, since the Phoenicians actually did buy up the corn-stores of Egypt, that granary of the ancient world, and housed the cargoes that were brought to them “upon great waters,” i.e., on the great Mediterranean. <hi type="italic">Sichor</hi> is a Hebraic form of <hi type="italic">Siris</hi> (the native name of the upper Nile, according to Dionysius Perieg. and Pliny). It signifies the black river (<hi type="italic">Meals</hi>, Eust. on Dion. Per. 222), the black slime of which gave such fertility to the land. “<hi type="italic">The harvest of the Nile</hi>” is not so much an explanation as an amplification. The valley of the Nile was the field for sowing and reaping, and the Phoenician coast was the barn for this valuable corn; and inasmuch as corn and other articles of trade were purchased and bartered there, it thereby became gain (constr. of <hi type="italic">sachar</hi>, Ewald, §213, a, used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">Pro 3:14</reference>), i.e., the means of gain, the source of profit or provision, to whole nations, and even to many such. Others render the word “emporium;” but <hi type="italic">sâchâr</hi> cannot have this meaning. Moreover, foreigners did not come to Phoenicia, but the Phoenicians went to them (Luzzatto).
entries.5824357c565bbb50336bc2cfaf7a0141ef99fd1e: <reference osisRef="Isa.23.4-Isa.23.5">Isa 23:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen13107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> The address to the whole of the coast-land now passes into an address to the ancestral city. <reference osisRef="Isa.23.4">Isa 23:4</reference> <hi type="italic">“Shudder, O Sidon; for the sea speaketh, the fortress of the sea, thus: I have not travailed, nor given birth, nor trained up young men, brought up maidens.”</hi> The sea, or more closely considered, the fortress of the sea, i.e., the rock-island on which Neo-tyrus stood with its strong and lofty houses, lifts up its voice in lamentation. Sidon, the ancestress of Canaan, must hear with overwhelming shame how Tyre mourns the loss of her daughters, and complains that, robbed as she has been of her children, she is like a barren women. For the war to have murdered her young men and maidens, was exactly the same as if she had never given birth to them or brought them up. Who is there that does not recognise in this the language of Isaiah (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa 1:2</reference>)? - Even in Egypt the fate of Phoenicia produces alarm. <reference osisRef="Isa.23.5">Isa 23:5</reference> <hi type="italic">“When the report cometh to Egypt, they tremble at the report from Tzor.”</hi> In the protasis (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.5">Isa 23:5</reference></hi>) <hi type="italic">lemitzraim</hi> (to Egypt) the verb “cometh” is implied; the <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.5">Isa 23:5</reference></hi> signifies simultaneousness, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Isa 18:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference> (Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 650). The news of the fall of Tyre spreads universal terror in Egypt, because its own prosperity depended upon Tyre, which was the great market for its corn; and when such a bulwark had fallen, a similar fate awaited itself.
entries.53fab310258642a5d07cdf2b630dfa557ba5229f: <reference osisRef="Isa.23.6-Isa.23.9">Isa 23:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13109" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Tyre, who desired to escape from death or transportation, are obliged to take refuge in the colonies, and the farther off the better: not in Cyprus, not in Carthage (as at the time when Alexander attacked the insular Tyre), but in Tartessus itself, the farthest off towards the west, and the hardest to reach. <hi type="italic">“Pass ye over to Tarshish; howl, ye inhabitants of the coast! Is this your fate, thou full of rejoicing, whose origin is from the days of the olden time, whom her feet carried far away to settle? Who hath determined such a thing concerning Tzor, the distributor of crowns, whose merchants are princes, whose traders are the chief men of the earth? Jehovah of hosts hath determined it, to desecrate the pomp of every kind of ornament, to dishonour the chief men of the earth, all of them.”</hi> The exclamation “howl ye” (<hi type="italic">hēillu</hi>) implies their right to give themselves up to their pain. In other cases complaint is unmanly, but here it is justifiable (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">Isa 15:4</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">Isa 23:7</reference></hi> the question arises, whether <hi type="italic">‛allizâh</hi> is a nominative predicate, as is generally assumed (<hi type="italic">“Is this, this deserted heap of ruins, your formerly rejoicing city?”</hi>), or a vocative. We prefer the latter, because there is nothing astonishing in the omission of the article in this case (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>; Ewald, 327,<hi type="italic">a</hi>); whereas in the former case, although it is certainly admissible (see <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference>), it is very harsh (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.16">Isa 14:16</reference>), and the whole expression a very doubtful one to convey the sense of לכם אשר עליזה קריה הזאת. To <hi type="italic">‛allizâh</hi> there is attached the descriptive, attributive clause: whose origin (<hi type="italic">kadmâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.55">Eze 16:55</reference>) dates from the days of the olden time; and then a second “whose feet brought her far away (<hi type="italic">raglaim</hi> construed as a masculine, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jer 13:16</reference>, for example) to dwell in a foreign land. This is generally understood as signifying transportation by force into an enemy’s country. But Luzzatto very properly objects to this, partly on the ground that רגליה יבלוּה (her feet carried her) is the strongest expression that can be used for voluntary emigration, to which <hi type="italic">lâgūr</hi> (to settle) also corresponds; and partly because we miss the antithetical ועתּה, which we should expect with this interpretation.
