entries.48e7b25b36e520ecb44537563699a58a761de355: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.12" sID="gen44070" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he said, Thou shalt not add any more to rejoice.</hi> <note n="112"> <div sID="gen44072" type="x-p"/> “And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice.” Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44073" type="x-p"/> FT370 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sous des tentes de peaux</foreign>;” — “Under tents of skins.”<div eID="gen44073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44074" type="x-p"/> FT371 “They raised up the palaces thereof.” — Eng. Ver. “Erected her palaces.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi>. Professor Alexander renders it, “They have roused up her palaces;” but says, “According to the usual interpretation, the <hi type="italic">towers</hi> mentioned are those used in ancient sieges; the masculine suffix refers to <foreign xml:lang="he">עם</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">gnām</hi>;) the feminine suffix to Tyre; and <foreign xml:lang="he">עורר</foreign> (<hi type="italic">gnōrēr</hi>) may be taken either in the sense of <hi type="italic">raising</hi>, (from <foreign xml:lang="he">ערר</foreign>, <hi type="italic">gnārăr</hi>,) or in that of <hi type="italic">rousing</hi>, (from <foreign xml:lang="he">עור</foreign>, <hi type="italic">gnūr</hi>,) that is, filling with confusion and alarm.”<div eID="gen44074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44075" type="x-p"/> FT372 “That is, of one kingdom. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.7.17 Bible:Dan.8.20">Daniel 7:17 8:20</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar began his conquests in the first year of his reign: from thence to the taking of Babylon by Cyrus are seventy years; at which time the nations conquered by Nebuchadnezzar were to be restored to liberty.” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi><div eID="gen44075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44076" type="x-p"/> FT373 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que le poete Horace s’est moqué d’une putain nommee <hi type="italic">Lydia</hi> pour la mesme occasion</foreign>;” — “That the Poet Horace mocked at a prostitute named <hi type="italic">Lydia</hi> for the same reason.”<div eID="gen44076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44077" type="x-p"/> FT374 “Tyre, after its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, recovered, as is here foretold, its ancient trade, wealth, and grandeur; as it did likewise after a second destruction by Alexander. It became Christian early with the rest of the neighboring countries. St. Paul himself found many Christians there. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.4">Acts 21:4</reference>.) It suffered much in the Diocletian persecution. It was an archbishopric under the patriarchate of Jerusalem, with fourteen bishoprics under its jurisdiction. It continued Christian till it was taken by the Saracens in 639; was recovered by the Christians in 1124; but in 1280 was conquered by the Mamalukes, and afterwards taken from them by the Turks in 1516. Since that time it has sunk into utter decay, is now a bare rock, ‘a place to spread nets upon,’ as the Prophet Ezekiel foretold it should be. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.26.14">Ezekiel 26:14</reference>.) See Sandy’s Travels; Vitringa on the place; Bishop Newton on the Prophecies, Dissert. xi.” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi><div eID="gen44077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44078" type="x-p"/> FT375 “The revenues of Tyre shall be employed in supporting the worshippers of the true God. The prophecy intimates that Tyre should be converted to the religion of Christ as it was in the earliest times of the gospel. Of the same event David also had prophesied in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.12 Bible:Ps.72.10 Bible:Ps.87.4">Psalm 45:12; 72:10; 87:4</reference>.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen44078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44079" type="x-p"/> FT376 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Afin qu’ils mangent leur saoul</foreign>;” — “That they may eat their fill.”<div eID="gen44079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44080" type="x-p"/> FT377 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Tout ce que nous employons pour la necessité de nos freres</foreign>;” — “All that we spend for relieving the want of our brethren.”<div eID="gen44080" type="x-p"/> </note> All this belongs to one and the same object; for, since a plain description would not have had sufficient weight, the Prophet confirms his prediction by many words. It was incredible that a city so celebrated and powerful, so well defended and fortified, and associated with many allies and confederates, should be destroyed and overturned. When he says, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not add</hi>, he does not intend to shut out the hope of restoration which he will give soon afterwards; for this threatening ought to be limited to the time of the ruin of Tyre, “Thou shalt not live wantonly, as formerly thou wert wont to do.”<div eID="gen44071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44081" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">O virgin.</hi> Metaphorically he calls her <hi type="italic">a virgin</hi>, because, previous to that time, the riches of Tyre were untouched, and had suffered no injury. This is not praise of chastity, but a witty manner of saying that the treasures which had been laid up in faithful custody will be violated. “Formerly thou didst skip lightly, like heifers in the bloom of youth; but when thou hast suffered violence, there will be an end of thy mirth;” just as if one should say, that the city of Venice has not lost her virginity because it has not been taken by force since it was built.<div eID="gen44081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44082" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Daughter of Sidon.</hi> He continues to speak of Tyre, but gives it this name, because it was built by the Sidonians, though the daughter excelled the mother, as frequently happens in human affairs. The convenience and situation of the place gave a superiority to the inhabitants of Tyre, and Sidon became but an appendage. From the book of Kings it is evident enough (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.1">1 Kings 5:1</reference>) that the monarchy of Tyre had a high reputation, but here the Prophet looked at its origin.<div eID="gen44082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44083" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Pass over to Chittim.</hi> When he bids them <hi type="italic">pass over to Chittim</hi>, he banishes them not only into Cilicia, but into countries still more distant; for under this name he includes Greece, Italy, and other countries; as if he had said, “When thou shalt change thy residence on account of banishment, thou shalt have no settled habitation in neighboring countries; but thou must wander through the whole world, shalt be dragged into unknown countries, and even there thou shalt find no rest.” Lastly, he means that the ruin will be so lamentable, that they will not have among neighbors, and, after crossing the sea, they will not have among foreigners, a place of rest.<div eID="gen44083" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44070" osisID="Isa.23.12" type="section"/>
entries.014f50eb066c460ccd24f1d65c8ddfc073df7151: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.13" sID="gen44084" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">Behold, the land of the Chaldeans. </hi>He now confirms by an example what he predicted about the taking of Tyre; for those things could scarcely obtain credit, especially among the inhabitants of Tyre, who thought that they were very far from such ruin. I am aware that this passage is explained in various ways, but I shall not spend time in refuting the opinions of others. It will be enough if I shall state, as far as I am able to form a judgment of it, the Prophet’s real meaning.<div eID="gen44085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44086" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The people of the Chaldeans was not;</hi> that is, they had no name; for, if we inquire into their origin, they were descended from the Assyrians, as is evident from <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.11">Genesis 10:11</reference>. He therefore says truly, that they were not at first a nation, but were concealed under the name of another, so that they did not form a separate body.<div eID="gen44086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44087" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Ashur founded it for the inhabitants of the wilderness.</hi> The words which we have rendered “inhabitants of the wilderness” others translate <hi type="italic">ships</hi>, but we do not approve of that exposition. What we at first stated is preferable, namely, that the Assyrians gave a settled condition to the Chaldeans, who formerly led a wandering life in the deserts under skins, <note n="113"> <div sID="gen44088" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44088" type="x-p"/> </note> but were collected into cities, and trained to higher civilization, by the Assyrians. This is also the meaning of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">עוררו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">gnōrĕrū</hi>,) namely, that they erected and built cities; for we cannot agree with those who render it “to destroy.” <note n="114"> <div sID="gen44089" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44089" type="x-p"/> </note> What happened?<div eID="gen44087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44090" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He brought it to ruin.</hi> That is, to use a common expression, “The daughter has devoured the mother;” for the Assyrian monarchy was overturned by the Chaldeans, though it was more powerful and flourishing than all the others. It will be said, what has this to do with Tyre? We answer, it is because Tyre will be overthrown by the Assyrians and Chaldeans. Since therefore the Chaldeans, who formerly were no people, could conquer the Assyrians and subject them to their power, why should we wonder if both united should conquer Tyre? Since the Lord gave such a display of his power in the case of the Assyrians, why should Tyre rely on her riches? She will undoubtedly be made to feel the hand of God, and her power will be of no avail to her.<div eID="gen44090" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44084" osisID="Isa.23.13" type="section"/>
entries.7950a1ad0c56e7d03415dd27e0895fcf21585f1e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.14" sID="gen44091" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi><hi type="italic"> Howl, ye ships of Tarshish.</hi> He repeats what he formerly said; for the Cilicians, on account of their vicinity, constantly traded with the inhabitants of Tyre. He bids their ships <hi type="italic">howl</hi>, because, when that harbour is shut up, the merchants will be struck with amazement at not having their ordinary intercourse. He calls that harbour which they visited, <hi type="italic">their strength</hi>, not only because it was a place of resort that might be relied on, but because there was no other way in which their voyages could yield profit.<div eID="gen44092" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44091" osisID="Isa.23.14" type="section"/>
entries.4f7b781939954cf4d3ecb43c4d297f1639caa97b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.15" sID="gen44093" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass in that day.</hi> After having spoken of the taking of Tyre, he next declares how long her calamity shall endure. It happens that cities which have been ruined are suddenly restored, and regain their former position; but the Prophet testifies that this city will be desolate and ruinous for <hi type="italic">seventy years</hi>. By <hi type="italic">being forgotten</hi> he means that there will be no merchandise, because she will not have the ordinary course of trade.<div eID="gen44094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44095" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">According to the days of one king.</hi> <note n="115"> <div sID="gen44096" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44096" type="x-p"/> </note> Some think that <hi type="italic">the days of one king</hi> relate to David, but that is exceedingly frivolous, for “the days of a king” are put for the age of a man, in the same manner as the age of a man is shewn by the Psalmist to be generally limited to seventy years. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.90.10">Psalm 90:10</reference>.) But why did he mention “a king” rather than any other man? It was because Tyre had a king, and reckoned time by the life of a king. This contributed greatly to establish the certainty of the prediction, for the Prophet could not have ascertained it by human conjectures.<div eID="gen44095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44097" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Tyre shall have a song like that of a harlot.</hi> By “the song of a harlot” he employs a beautiful comparison to denote merchandise; not that in itself it ought to be condemned, for it is useful and necessary to a commonwealth, but he alludes to the fraud and dishonesty with which it frequently abounds, so that it may justly be compared to the occupation of a harlot.<div eID="gen44097" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44093" osisID="Isa.23.15" type="section"/>
entries.7e5fe68b6a97436c118d5967583cd85ab6e449e7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.16" sID="gen44098" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">Take a harp.</hi> He compares Tyre to a harlot, who, after having spent the whole period of her youth in debauchery, has at length grown old, and on that account is forsaken and despised by all, and yet cannot forget her former gain and lewdness, but desires to grow young again and renew her loves, and, in order to attract men, goes about the city, delighting their ears by songs and musical instruments. Such prostitutes are seized with some kind of madness, when they perceive that they are disregarded on account of their old age; and we see that Horace mocks at Lydia on this account. <note n="116"> <div sID="gen44100" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44100" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus Tyre, after having been ruined, and as it were buried in oblivion, will again put forth her efforts, and schemes, and contrivances, for recovering her former condition.<div eID="gen44099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44101" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Make sweet melody.</hi> By the “harp” and “sweet melody,” he means the tricks, and frauds, and blandishments, and flatteries of merchants, by which they impose on men, and as it were drive them into their nets. In a word, he shews by what methods mercantile cities become rich, that is, by deceitful and unlawful methods; and therefore he says, that Tyre will regale their ears by pleasant melody.<div eID="gen44101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44102" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Sing many songs.</hi> That is, Tyre will add fraud to fraud, and allurements to allurements, that at length she may attract all to her, may be again remembered by men, and recover her former celebrity. In short, as an old harlot contrives methods for regaining the favor of men, and allures them by painting, and ornaments, and dress, and songs, and musical instruments, so will Tyre recover her wealth and power by the same arts with which she formerly succeeded. And yet he does not on that account exhort Tyre to restore herself in this way, but proceeds with his prophecy.<div eID="gen44102" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44098" osisID="Isa.23.16" type="section"/>
entries.6eba2ca2149c59dfffa531dfb91f5b626dea8461: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.23.17" sID="gen44103" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">Jehovah will visit Tyre.</hi> <note n="117"> <div sID="gen44105" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44105" type="x-p"/> </note> Although the Lord will afflict Tyre in such a manner that she will appear to be ruined, yet he declares that she will obtain mercy, because, rising at length out of her ruins, she will be restored to her former vigor. Such a restoration is justly ascribed to the favor of God; for otherwise the same thing must have happened to them as Malachi foretells would happen to the Edomites, that the Lord would overturn and destroy all that men would build. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.1.4">Malachi 1:4</reference>.) Consequently they would never have returned to their former condition if the Lord had not aided them.<div eID="gen44104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44106" type="x-p"/>From these words we ought to draw a profitable doctrine, that though the Lord is a severe judge towards the wicked, yet he leaves room for the exercise of his compassion, and is never so harsh as not to mitigate his chastisements, and at length to put an end to them. And if he is such towards the wicked, what will he be towards those whom he has adopted, and on whom he determines to pour out his goodness? When kingdoms therefore are re-established, when cities are rebuilt, and nations regain their freedom, this is brought about solely by the providence of God, who, whenever he pleases, lays low what is high, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.7">1 Samuel 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.52">Luke 1:52</reference>,) and quickly raises up and restores what was fallen.<div eID="gen44106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44107" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And then she will return to her hire.</hi> This ought to be viewed as a contrast to the former statement, for the meaning is, that Tyre will be no better, and will not be reformed by so severe a chastisement, because she will quickly return to her natural disposition; for he accuses her of ingratitude. We see instances of the same kind every day. There is scarcely a corner of the world in which the Lord has not exhibited proofs of his judgment. To those whom he has chastised he allows time to breathe, but they become no better. Isaiah says that this will happen to Tyre.<div eID="gen44107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44108" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">She will commit fornication.</hi> “She will not repent, but, on the contrary, will return to her former courses. <hi type="italic">She will commit fornication</hi>, as she was formerly accustomed to do.” He unquestionably speaks of buying and selling, but continues to employ the comparison which he had adopted; not that he wishes to condemn the occupation of a merchant, as we have already said, but that it is so largely mingled with the corruption of men as to resemble closely the life of a harlot; for it is so full of tricks, and hidden stratagems, and deep-laid traps, (as we often see,) that it appears to have been contrived for the purpose of ensnaring and deceiving men. How many new and unheard of contrivances for making gain and exacting usury are every day invented, which no one who has not been long trained in the school of merchandise can understand? We need not wonder, therefore, that the Prophet made use of this comparison, for it means that Tyre will have no more honesty than before in mercantile transactions.<div eID="gen44108" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.23.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44103" osisID="Isa.23.17" type="section"/>
entries.ae38ff34fa4a83a3986d06648716fc46c982df5d:
18. But her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the Lord. This was another instance of the divine compassion towards Tyre. Though she had been restored, yet she was not converted to God, but continued to follow dishonest practices, so that she justly deserved to be ruined. And indeed she was again punished severely, when Alexander took the city by storm; but still the kingdom of Christ, as Luke informs us, was erected there. (Acts 21:4.) This verse ought therefore to be viewed as contrasted with the former, as if he had said, “And yet the merchandise of Tyre shall be consecrated to God.” Here we have an astonishing proof of the goodness of God, which penetrated not only into this abominable brothel, but almost into hell itself. The restoration of Tyre ought thus to be regarded as a proof of the goodness of God; but the former favor was small in comparison with the second, when God consecrated her to himself.
But a question arises, “Could that which the inhabitants of Tyre obtained by cheating and unlawful methods be offered to God in sacrifice?” For God abhors such sacrifices, and demands an honest and pure conscience. (Proverbs 21:27, Isaiah 1:13.) Many commentators, in expounding this passage, give themselves much uneasiness about this question, but without any good reason; for the Prophet does not mean that the merchandise of Tyre will be consecrated to God while she continues to commit fornication, but describes a time subsequent to her change and conversion. At that time she will not lay up riches for herself, will not amass them by unlawful methods, but will employ them in the service of God, and will spend the produce of her merchandise in relieving the wants of the godly. When he used a word expressive of what was disgraceful, he had his eye on the past, but intimated that she would unlearn those wicked practices, and change her disposition.
It shall not be treasured nor laid up. He describes, in a few words, the repentance of Tyre, who, having formerly been addicted to avarice, has been converted to Christ, and will no longer labor to amass riches, but will employ them in kind and generous actions; and this is the true fruit of repentance, as Paul admonishes, that “he who stole should steal no more, but, on the contrary, should labor that he might relieve the poor and needy.” (Ephesians 4:28.) Isaiah foretells that the inhabitants of Tyre, who formerly, through insatiable avarice, devoured the riches of all, will henceforth take pleasure in generous actions, because they will no longer have an insatiable desire of gain. It is an evidence of brotherly love when we relieve our neighbors, as it is an evidence of cruelty if we suffer them to be hungry, especially when we ourselves have abundance.
Her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the Lord. He next mentions a proper method of exercising generosity, which is, to employ their wealth in aiding the servants of God. Though he includes all godly persons, yet he alludes to the Levites and priests, some of whom sacrificed, while others made ready the sacrifices, and others kept watch, and, in short, all were ready to perform their duty; and therefore they were said to “dwell before the Lord.” (Numbers 3 and 4.) The same thing may justly be said of all the ministers of the Church. But as all believers, of whatever rank they are, belong to the sanctuary of God, and have been made by Christ “a royal priesthood,” (1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6,) that they may stand in the presence of God, so I willingly regard this passage as relating to all “the household of faith,” (Galatians 6:10,) to whom attention is especially due; for Paul holds them out as having the highest claims, and enjoins that they shall be first relieved. If the tie which binds us universally to mankind ought to prevent us from “despising our own flesh,” (Isaiah 58:7,) how much more the tie that binds the members of Christ, which is closer and more sacred than any natural bonds?
We ought also to attend to this mode of expression, by which we are said to “dwell before God;”
{Bogus footnote}
for though there is not now any “Ark of the Covenant,” (Hebrews 9:4,) yet, through the kindness of Christ, we approach more nearly to God than the Levites formerly did. We are therefore enjoined to “walk before him,” as if we were under his eye, that we may follow holiness and justice with a pure conscience. We are enjoined to walk before him, and always to consider him as present, that we may be just and upright.
That they may eat till they are satisfied.
{Bogus footnote}
The Prophet means that we ought to supply the wants of brethren with greater abundance and generosity than what is customary among men; for when neighbors ought to be relieved, men are very niggardly. Few men perform cheerfully any gratuitous duty, or labor, or kindness; for they reckon that they give up and take from their own property all that they bestow on others. For the purpose of correcting this error, God highly commends cheerfulness; for the command which Paul gives to deacons, “to distribute joyfully,” (Romans 12:8,) ought to be applied to all; and all ought to remember that passage which declares that “God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7.)
It deserves our attention, also, that the Prophet says that what is bestowed on the poor is consecrated to God; as the Spirit elsewhere teaches, that “with such sacrifices God is well pleased.” (Hebrews 13:16; 2 Corinthians 9:12.) Never was it on his own account that he commanded sacrifices to be made, nor did he ever stand in need of them. But under the law he ordained such exercises of piety; and he now commands us to bestow and spend on our neighbors something that is our own, and declares that all that we lay out on their account
{Bogus footnote}
is “a sacrifice of sweet savor,” (Philippians 4:18,) and is approved and accepted by him. This ought powerfully to inflame us to the exercise of kindness and generosity, when we learn that our alms are so highly applauded, and that our hands, as well as our gift, are consecrated to God.
CHAPTER 24
Isaiah Chapter 24:1-23
1. Behold, the Lord maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.
1. Ecce Iehova evacuat terram, denudat eam, evertit faciem ejus, et incolas ejus dissipat.
2. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
2. Et erit ut populus, ita sacerdos; ut servus, ita domina ejus; ut ancilla, ita domina ejus; ut emptor, ita venditor; ut mutuo dans, ita qui mutuo accipit; ut foenerator, ita qui accipit foenori, (vel, ut creditor, ita debitor.)
3. The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled: for the Lord hath spoken this word.
3. Evacuando evacuabitur terra, et direptione diripietur; quoniam Iehova pronunciavit hoc verbum.
4. The earth mourneth and fadeth away; the world languisheth and fadeth away; the haughty people of the earth do languish.
4. Luxit, cecidit terra; elanguit, cecidit orbis; elanguerunt qui erant sublimis populus terræ.
5. The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.
5. Et terra fallax fuit sub incolis suis; quoniam transgressi sunt leges, mutarunt statutum, dissolverunt foedus seculi.
6. Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left.
6. Itaque maledictio cosumpsit terram, et desolati sunt incolæ ejus; ideo combusti sunt, inquam, incolæ terræ; et pauci residui sunt facti homines.
7. The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merry hearted do sigh.
7. Periit vinum, elanguit vitis, gemuerunt omnes qui læto erant corde.
8. The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.
8. Cessavit gaudium tympanorum, desiit strepitus exultantium, quievit lætitia citharæ.
9. They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it.
9. Cum cantico non bibent vinum; amara erit sicera bibentibus eam.
10. The city of confusion is broken down; every house is shut up, that no man may come in.
10. Contrita est civitas vanitatis; clausa est omnis domus, ne quis ingrediatur.
11 There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone.
11. Clamor est super vino in plateis; obscuratum est omne gaudium; migravit lætitia terræ.
12. In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction.
12. Residua est in urbe vastitas, et vastatione percussa est porta.
13. When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be as the shaking of an olive tree, and as the gleaning-grapes when the vintage is done.
13. Quia sic erit in medio terræ, in medio populorum, quasi decussio olivæ, et quasi racemi, cum peracta est vindemia.
14. They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the Lord, they shall cry aloud from the sea.
14. Hi levabunt vocem suam; jubilabunt in altitudine Iehovæ, vociferabuntur a mari.
15. Wherefore glorify ye the Lord in the fires, even the name of the Lord God of Israel in the isles of the sea.
15. Propterea in vallibus glorificate Iehovam, in insulis maris nomen Iehovæ Dei Israel.
16. From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.
16. Ab extremo terræ laudes audivimus, gloriam (vel, gratulationem) justo, et dixi, Macies mihi, macies mihi, væ mihi. Prævaricatores prævaricati sunt; prævaricatione, inquam, prævaricatores prævaricati sunt.
17. Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth.
17. Pavor, et fovea, et laqueus super te, O icola terræ.
18. And it shall come to pass, that he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake.
18. Et accidet ut qui effugerit a voce pavoris, incidat in foveam; et qui ascenderit e medio foveæ capiatur laqueo. Quoniam fenestræ de excelso apertæ sunt; et commota sunt fundamenta terræ.
19. The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly.
19. Contritione contrita est terra; dissolutione dissoluta est terra; commotione commota est terra.
20. The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.
20. Agitatione agitata est terra, sicut ebrius; et transferetur sicut tabernaculum; et gravis erit super eam iniquitas ejus; et corruet, neque adjiciet ut resurgat.
21. And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall punish the host of the high ones that are on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth.
21. Et erit in die illa, visitabit Iehova super exercitum excelsum in excelso, et super reges terræ super terram.
22. And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited.
22. Et congregabuntur congregatione instar vinctorum in carcere, et claudentur in ergastulo; deinde post multos dies visitabuntur.
23. Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.
23. Erubescet luna, et pudefiet sol; cum regnaverit Iehova exercituum in monte Sion, et in Ierusalem; et coram senibus suis gloria.

                        </ns0:gap>

Zech. 9. 2, 4.</ns0:note> THe burden of Tyre <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Prophecy of the heavy Calamity and Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyre;</ns0:hi> which now stood in its Strength and Glory, being seated in an Island, upon a Rock, abounding in Riches, mighty in Naval Power, having lately conquered that Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vy which the <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> brought against them. Yet this City was, according to this Prophecy, destroyed; and that twice, first by <ns0:hi>Nebuc<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>adnezzar,</ns0:hi> and long afterward by <ns0:hi>Alexander the Great.</ns0:hi> And although this Prophecy seem directly and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly to respect the former Destruction, yet it seems to have some reference to the latter also; onely it is intima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, That after seventy years <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> should recover her for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer Power and Glory, before her second and final Destru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction.</ns0:note>. Howl, ye ships <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either, 1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> properly; to which Howling and La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />menting is ascribed by a known Figure called <ns0:hi>Prosopopaeia:</ns0:hi> or, 2. Metanymically, the Merchants and Owners of Ships, who had much Commerce with this illustrious Mart.</ns0:note> of Tarshish <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. of <ns0:hi>Tarsa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> a great Port of <ns0:hi>Cilicia,</ns0:hi> which anciently had the Dominion of that part of the Sea: or, 2. of the Ocean, which is so called 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 10. 22. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 48. 8. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 2. 16.</ns0:note>, for it is laid waste <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It shall shortly be laid waste; Which was ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filled not by <ns0:hi>Shalmanezer,</ns0:hi> as some would have it; for though he straitned it for some time, yet he never took it; but by <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, so that there is no house, no entring in <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">So effectually wasted, that there is not an House left in it, nor any Merchants or others that go into it, either to Trade in it, or to repair it.</ns0:note>: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The sence of the Words thus rendred may be this, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>, i. e.</ns0:hi> this Burden or Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyre, is. i. e.</ns0:hi> shall be, <ns0:hi>revealed,</ns0:hi> declared or made known, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>;</ns0:hi> either, 1. to the <ns0:hi>Tyre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans,</ns0:hi> to whom this Notice should be sent concerning the Preparations of their Enemies against them: or, 2. to the Ships, by which he means their Owners or Merchants, <ns0:hi>from the land of Chittim:</ns0:hi> which may be here mentioned either because they first had and gave them notice of it, as was now said; or, because their last and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>orest Destruction was brought upon them by <ns0:hi>Alexander,</ns0:hi> who was <ns0:hi>of the land of Chittim,</ns0:hi> as is affirmed by that very ancient and venerable, though Apocryphal Writer, 1 <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 1. 1. & 8. 5. But this Place is otherwise rendred, both by ancient and later Interpreters, which seems to be more natural and easie, and no less agreeable to the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text; either thus, <ns0:hi>that she is laid waste, so that there is no house, nor entring</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>coming in</ns0:hi> (to wit, for Traffick) <ns0:hi>from the land of Chittim, is made known to them,</ns0:hi> to wit, to the Ships or Merchants that used to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sort thither for Traffick: or rather thus, <ns0:hi>for it is laid waste<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> so that there is no house,</ns0:hi> (not any Houses left for the Citi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zens to dwell in) <ns0:hi>nor entring</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>coming in</ns0:hi> (to wit, of Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chants) <ns0:hi>from the land of Chittim: she</ns0:hi> (to wit, her People) <ns0:hi>is removed or gone into captivity,</ns0:hi> as this Word properly signifies, and is rendred <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 38. 12. And for the last <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Word, <ns0:hi>lamo,</ns0:hi> which is rendred <ns0:hi>to them</ns0:hi> (which is the onely Objection against this Interpretation) it is onely added as an Elegan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cie of the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Language, and hath no further Significa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, as it is also <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 58. 7. and as the Particle <ns0:hi>lo,</ns0:hi> which signifies the same thing, and such other Pronouns, are fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently redundant and insignificant in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text, as hath been oft observed by <ns0:hi>Grammarians</ns0:hi> and Interpreters. He mentions <ns0:hi>the land of Chittim,</ns0:hi> because this was an eminent Place for Shipping and Trading, as is manifest from <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 24. 24. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 27. 6. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 11. 30. and therefore doubtless had great Dealings and Commerce with <ns0:hi>Tyre,</ns0:hi> and may here be put Synechdochically for all other Countries which Traded with her. It is not necessary, for the understanding of this Text, to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> what <ns0:hi>Chittim</ns0:hi> is, whether it was <ns0:hi>Italy,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Greece,</ns0:hi> or the Islands in those Parts; it is sufficient to know, that it was a Seafaring Place in the <ns0:hi>Midland Sea,</ns0:hi> and so much startled and concerned in the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyre.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> silent.</ns0:note> still <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Be silent,</ns0:hi> as one confounded, and not knowing what to say; or as Mourners use to be, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 2. 8, 13. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 47. 5. boast no more of thy Wealth and Power, as thou usedst to do.</ns0:note> ye inhabitants of the isle <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. of <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> which now was an Island, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 27. 3. & 28. 2. till <ns0:hi>Alexander</ns0:hi> joined it to the Conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent, as <ns0:hi>Pliny</ns0:hi> reports. Although the Title of <ns0:hi>Islands</ns0:hi> is oft given by the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> to Places bordering upon the Sea.</ns0:note>, thou whom the merchants of Zidon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">An eminent City of <ns0:hi>Palestina,</ns0:hi> nigh unto <ns0:hi>Tyre,</ns0:hi> much con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerned with her and for her.</ns0:note>, that pass over the sea <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That are a Seafaring Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple.</ns0:note>, have replenished <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">With Mariners, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 27. 8. and Commodities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And by great waters <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By the Sea, which is very fitly called <ns0:hi>the great waters, Psal.</ns0:hi> 107. 23. understand, <ns0:hi>cometh,</ns0:hi> or is brought to her.</ns0:note> the seed of Sihor <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Corn of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> wherewith <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> abounded, and fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished divers other Parts of the World, whence it was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led the Granary of the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Empire; which also was ea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sily conveyed by Sea from <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Tyre,</ns0:hi> and thence to di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers other Countries. This is called <ns0:hi>seed</ns0:hi> here, as also <ns0:hi>Hag.</ns0:hi> 2. 19. and elsewhere, by an usual <ns0:hi>Metonymy;</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the seed of Sihor,</ns0:hi> because it grew up the more abundantly because of the Overflow of the River, as all sorts of Authors have no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted. For <ns0:hi>Sihor</ns0:hi> is nothing else but <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> as appears from <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 2. 18. which is called <ns0:hi>Sihor,</ns0:hi> as by the <ns0:hi>Greeks</ns0:hi> it was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>Melas,</ns0:hi> from its black Colour. And this and no other River seems to be that <ns0:hi>Sihor</ns0:hi> which is so oft mentioned as one of the Bounds of the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 34. 5. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> because that Land, at least in that extent which God allot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted and gave it to the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> though they through ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />glect or cowardise might not actually possess it, did reach to one of the Branches of that River: And indeed, if <ns0:hi>Sihor</ns0:hi> be not <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> that great and neighbouring River is not na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med in all the Scripture, which seems very improbable.</ns0:note>, the harvest of the river <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This Clause explains the former; that plentiful Harvest of Corn which comes from the Influence and Inundation of <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> which is emphatically called <ns0:hi>the river,</ns0:hi> as here, so also <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 1. 22. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 19. 5. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 29. 3, 9. as <ns0:hi>Euphrates</ns0:hi> is in other Texts of Scripture.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> her revenue <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Is as easily procured, and plentifully enjoyed by her, as if it grew in her own Terri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tories.</ns0:note>, and she is a mart of nations <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A Place to which all Nations resort for Traffick.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Be thou ashamed, O Zidon <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>Zidon</ns0:hi> was a great City near <ns0:hi>Tyre,</ns0:hi> and strongly united to her by Commerce and League, and called by some the Mother of <ns0:hi>Tyre,</ns0:hi> which, they say, was built and first inhabited by a Colony of the <ns0:hi>Sidonians;</ns0:hi> and therefore she must needs be greatly concerned in the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyrus.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>; for the sea <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That part of the Sea in which <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> was, and from which Ships and Men were sent into all Countries.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:585" />
hath spoken, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the strength of the sea <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This is added to explain what he meant by <ns0:hi>the sea,</ns0:hi> even <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> who might be called <ns0:hi>the strength of the Sea,</ns0:hi> either actively, because it defended that part of the Sea from Pyracies and Injuries; or passively, because it was defended and streng<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thened by the Sea, which encompassed it. And this Title is here given to <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> to shew what great cause of Confu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion and Fear <ns0:hi>Sidon</ns0:hi> had from this Example, which for Strength was much inferiour to <ns0:hi>Tyrus.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, I travel not, nor bring forth children, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther do I nourish up young men, <ns0:hi>nor</ns0:hi> bring up virgins <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I who was so ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding fruitful and populous, that I sent forth Colonies into other Countries, (of which the famous City of <ns0:hi>Carthage</ns0:hi> was one) am now become barren and desolate.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 As at the report concerning Egypt, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">According to this Translation the sence is, All the neighbouring Nations shall be no less terrified at the Ti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dings of the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> than they were of old upon the Report of God's former and dreadful Judgments upon the <ns0:hi>Egyptians;</ns0:hi> of which see <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 14, 15, 16. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 2. 9, 11. because they shall despair of resisting that Enemy against whom that vast and potent City, which was deemed impregnable, could not defend it self. But the Words are by the <ns0:hi>Seventy,</ns0:hi> and other both ancient and later Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters, rendred otherwise, and that very agreeably to the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text, <ns0:hi>When the report</ns0:hi> (to wit, of the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Tyre</ns0:hi>) came, or shall come, (which Word is easily under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, as it is above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. and in other Texts of Scripture before mentioned) <ns0:hi>to the Egyptians, they shall be sorely pained according to the report of Tyre;</ns0:hi> their Grief shall be answera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to the Report; as the Report is very dreadful, so their Grief and Anguish shall be very great: or, they shall fear lest they should be destroyed in like manner as <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> was destroyed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Pass ye over to Tarshish <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Flee from your own Country to <ns0:hi>Tarsus</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Cilicia,</ns0:hi> and there bewail your Calamities. Or, rather, as others render the Place, <ns0:hi>Pass over the sea,</ns0:hi> which is oft called <ns0:hi>Tarshish;</ns0:hi> of which see on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>, howl ye inhabi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tants of the isle <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> as before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> this your joyous <ns0:hi>city</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That formerly lived in so much Pomp, and Pleasure, and Security.</ns0:note>, whose antiquity is of ancient days <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Being built before <ns0:hi>Ioshua</ns0:hi>'s time, as is ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifest from <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 19. 29.</ns0:note>? her own feet shall carry her<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Whereas before, like a delicate Lady, she would not set the Sole of her Foot to the ground, as the Expression is <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 56. but used to be carried in stately Chariots, or magnificent Vessels.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from afar off.</ns0:note> afar off to sojourn<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To seek for new Habitations. For, as some of the <ns0:hi>Tyrians</ns0:hi> were taken and carried Captive into <ns0:hi>Chaldea</ns0:hi> and other Places, so others fled by Sea into several Parts of the World, <ns0:hi>Carthage,</ns0:hi> and divers other Towns of the <ns0:hi>Midland Sea,</ns0:hi> as is recorded by ancient Historians.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre<ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Words of Admiration: Who and where is he that could imagine or durst attempt such a thing as this? This is the Work of God, as is expressed <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. and not of Man.</ns0:note>, the crowning <ns0:hi>city</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which was a Royal City, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 25. 22. and called <ns0:hi>a king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, Ezek.</ns0:hi> 28. 2, 12. and carried away the Crown from all other Cities, and Crowned her self and her Citizens with Glory and Delights.</ns0:note>, whose merchants <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces<ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Equal to Princes for Wealth, and Power, and Reputation.</ns0:note>, whose traffiquers are the honourable of the earth?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 The LORD of hosts hath purposed it<ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This is the Lord's own doing; therefore do not doubt it, nor wonder at it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to pol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lute.</ns0:note> to stain the pride of all glory, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> to bring in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to contempt all the honourable of the earth<ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">God's Design is by this one Exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple to abate and abase the Pride of all the Potentates of the Earth, that they may see and know what weak and wretched Creatures they are, when God leaves them, and sets himself against them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Pass through thy land <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Tarry no longer in thy own Territories, but flee through them, and beyond them, into other Countries, for Safety and Relief.</ns0:note> as a river<ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Swiftly, lest you be prevented; and continually, till you be all gone; and in Sholes and Multi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tudes.</ns0:note>, O daughter of Tarshish <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">O <ns0:hi>Tyrus;</ns0:hi> for of her he speaks both in the fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />going and following Words. And <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> might well be cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>the daughter of Tarshish, i. e.</ns0:hi> of the Sea, as that Word is used <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. and elsewhere, because it then was an Island, and therefore as it were born of the Sea, and nourished and brought up by it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no more <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> girdle.</ns0:note> strength<ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>no more girdle.</ns0:hi> the Girdle, which strengthens the Loins of a Man, is put for Strength, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 12. 21. & 38. 3. It behoveth you, O People of <ns0:hi>Ty<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rus,</ns0:hi> to flee away, as I advise you; for your City is unable to defend you; your Wealth, the Sinews of War, is lost; your Walls broken down; the Sea, which, like a Girdle, surrounded and defended you, is now in part filled up by your Enemies, who have joined you to the main Land; your former Friends and Allies forsake you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 He <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Lord, expressed <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note> stretched out his hand <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To strike it, the Antece<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent being put for the Consequent.</ns0:note> over the sea<ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>against the sea; i. e.</ns0:hi> against <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> the Daughter of the Sea, as she was now called; and consequently against all those Ships and Men which used to Traffique with <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> and were enriched by that Trade, and therefore suffered in her Fall.</ns0:note>, he shook the kingdoms<ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>He made the kingdoms to tremble;</ns0:hi> either, 1. the two Kingdoms of <ns0:hi>Tyre</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sidon;</ns0:hi> or rather, 2. the neighbouring and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />federate Kingdoms, as appears by comparing this with <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 26. 15, 16, 17, 18. who might justly quake at her Fall, partly for the dreadfulness and unexpectedness of the thing; partly because <ns0:hi>Tyre</ns0:hi> was a Bulwark, and a Refuge, and a great Advantage to them; and partly because her Fall made way for their Ruine, as being destroyed by their Common Enemy.</ns0:note>: the LORD hath given a commandment <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Hath contrived and purposed it, as was said <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 9. hath put this Design into the Heads and Hearts of her Enemies, and given them Courage to at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt, and Strength to execute so difficult an Enterprise.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing a mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chant-man.</ns0:note> against <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                     <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>against Canaan:</ns0:hi> the Word <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> being taken either, 1. for a <ns0:hi>merchant,</ns0:hi> as it is used <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 41. 6. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 12. 7. or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 2. for the Proper Name of a Place or People, as it is generally used: for the <ns0:hi>Tyrians</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sidonians</ns0:hi> were descended from <ns0:hi>Canaan, Gen.</ns0:hi> 10. 15. and were the onely considerable Remainders of that cursed Race whom God had devoted to Destruction.                   <ns0:p n="12">12 And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">So he calls her, either for her Pride and Beauty, and living in great Ease and Pleasure; or because she had hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therto never born the yoke of a conquering Enemy: though withal he declares, that she should be <ns0:hi>oppressed</ns0:hi> or deflowred very suddenly.</ns0:note>, daughter of Zidon<ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Whereby he understands ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. <ns0:hi>Zidon</ns0:hi> her self, who suffered in and with <ns0:hi>Tyre;</ns0:hi> for so this Phrase seems generally to be used, <ns0:hi>the daughter of Sion,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>of Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>of Babel,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Egypt, &c.</ns0:hi> being nothing else but <ns0:hi>Sion, Ierusalem, Babel, Egypt, &c.</ns0:hi> or rather, 2. <ns0:hi>Tyrus,</ns0:hi> as most Interpreters both Jewish and Christian understand it, of whom this whole Context and Prophecy speaks; which may well be called <ns0:hi>the daughter of Zidon,</ns0:hi> because she was first built and possessed by a Colony of the <ns0:hi>Sidonians;</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Pliny</ns0:hi> calleth <ns0:hi>Carthage</ns0:hi> the Daughter of <ns0:hi>Tyre<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>

people was not<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Chal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deans</ns0:hi> at first were not a People, not formed into any Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monwealth or Kingdom.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>till</ns0:hi> the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Till <ns0:hi>Nimrod,</ns0:hi> the Head and Founder of the <ns0:hi>Assyrian</ns0:hi> Monarchy, built <ns0:hi>Babel, Gen.</ns0:hi> 10, 9. now the Head of the <ns0:hi>Chaldean</ns0:hi> Monarchy, which he built for those People, who then lived in Tents, and were disper<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed here and there in wild and waste Places, that he might bring them into Order, and under Government, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by establish and promote his own Empire.</ns0:note>: they set up the towers thereof, they raised up the palaces thereof<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Chal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deans</ns0:hi> being by this means brought together into a Body, fell to the Work of Building their City, and its Towers and Palaces, and thereby got Power and Dominion over their Neighbours, till at last they grew the greatest of all the Monarchies that then were upon Earth.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Lord, who is expressed before, and is frequently designed in Scripture by this indefinite Pronoun <ns0:hi>he,</ns0:hi> as hath been many times ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served: Whereby he insinuates the true Reason why nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> nor the <ns0:hi>Tyrians</ns0:hi> should be able to stand, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Almighty God was engaged against them.</ns0:note> brought it to ruine<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Will infallibly bring that great Empire to ruine.
